https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/absolutel.text: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent Updated Fri, 24 July 2026 at 3:39 pm UTC 1 John Hajdu outside the Imperial War Museum in London. John is loaning his beloved teddy for the Childhood in War exhibition, which opens on 31 July.Photograph: Richard Ash/© IWM When John Hajdu was three, his parents gave him a teddy bear small enough to fit into his hands: 86 years later, it is the only surviving object from his childhood. The bear, which the 89-year-old simply calls “teddy”, stayed with him as his father was taken to a labour camp, his mother sent to a concentration camp, and he hid in a non-Jewish neighbour’s cupboard before being forced into the Budapest ghetto. From 31 July, teddy will go on public display for the first time as part of Childhood in War , a new exhibition at the Imperial War Museum, London, examining how conflict shapes children’s lives. Displayed in a recreated second world war bedroom, the bear sits among toys, books and personal possessions that ask visitors to consider what childhood looks like when play, education and family life are disrupted by war. The exhibition combines hundreds of objects with immersive environments, including a full-size railway carriage, a wartime classroom and a cold war living room and kitchen, alongside testimonies from children living through conflicts in places including Ukraine, Sudan and Afghanistan. For Hajdu, teddy represents a childhood interrupted. Before the war, his life was typical of a well-to-do, middle-class Jewish family. By 1944, after years of antisemitic persecution in Hungary, his father had been sent to a labour camp and Hajdu and his mother had been forced into a designated yellow-star house. Teddy did, and still does, mean so much to me. It was my only connection to a family life I barely remembered John Hajdu “We could only take with us what we could carry, and that meant just a few pieces of clothing and teddy,” he says. “There was absolutely no chance of being a kid. I had no other toys or books. We were only allowed out in the afternoon wearing the yellow star. I couldn’t meet other children. We weren’t allowed in parks, cinemas or swimming pools or cafes. I was completely isolated.” The exhibition explores exactly those everyday losses. A reconstructed classroom shows how war disrupts children’s education through objects from conflicts including the second world war, Northern Ireland, Afghanistan and the former Yugoslavia. There are comics warning children about landmines and unexploded ordnance. Visitors can also climb into an evacuee train carriage containing letters sent home and Kindertransport objects, including a red knitted jumper given to Jochewet Heidenstein by her parents before she and her sisters fled Berlin for Britain. In October 1944, Hajdu’s mother was arrested and taken to Mauthausen concentration camp in Austria. Believing she would never return, Hajdu’s aunt rushed him into the cupboard of a non-Jewish neighbour. Related: Children are the longest-lasting casualties of war “I had teddy in my pocket,” he says. “I was in complete darkness and had to keep completely quiet. It seemed like a very long time, which was an incredibly frightening experience for a seven-year-old … By that time I was able to comprehend what happened without fully understanding the enormity of the situation.” He later moved with his aunt into the Budapest ghetto, sharing a flat with more than 20 strangers. “There were no children. We survived on horse meat and bread. Dead bodies lay piled up on the streets, having died of cold, starvation or disease. I was always hungry. Again, I had teddy in my pocket.” The ghetto was liberated by Soviet troops in January 1945, just before retreating German forces planned to destroy it. Miraculously, Hajdu was reunited with both his parents. His mother survived Mauthausen after US troops liberated the camp, but returned with broken ribs, smashed teeth and lasting psychological scars. “I was convinced I’d never see my parents again,” he says. A decade later, after the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising, Hajdu and his mother walked 40km (25 miles) and crossed an icy river under cover of darkness to reach Austria. They arrived in Britain in 1957 on a Red Cross train, with teddy travelling with them. Throughout the exhibition, stories such as Hajdu’s sit alongside contemporary accounts from children living through war today. Visitors can explore a 360-degree virtual tour of an underground school in Ukraine created by one of its pupils, read poems written by Ukrainian children for Unicef’s Poems for Peace project , and see drawings by children in Sudan that were later submitted as evidence of alleged war crimes to the international criminal court. A poem by a 15-year-old Afghan girl describes the moment the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in August 2021: “I witnessed how that day darkened not only Kabul’s sky, but also the dreams and hopes of so many.” The exhibition also examines how childhood can become politicised, with material from the Hitler Youth and Soviet Komsomol movements. “We wanted to talk about the impact of war on children’s lives,” says curator Fran Singleton. “With more conflicts in the news at the moment, it felt like the right time to create an exhibition that offers families a space to come together and discuss these important topics.” Related: ‘Into the arms of strangers’: child refugees of Nazi Germany remember For Hajdu, allowing teddy to leave his home for the first time has been surprisingly difficult. “Teddy did, and still does, mean so much to me. It was my only connection to a family life I barely remembered when I was three,” he says. “I find it difficult to look at the desk where he normally sits.” Now a grandfather of four, Hajdu spends much of his time speaking in schools about surviving the Holocaust. As the number of survivors dwindles, he hopes younger generations will continue telling these stories. “I tell them, ‘When you go home, talk to your grandparents and parents. Find out whether they’ve gone through traumas, whether it’s in Asia or Africa.’ “My small story is an example that you can survive. Unfortunately, people are suffering all over the world. We are getting older, and fewer and fewer Holocaust survivors are here to tell these stories. It’s absolutely vital that the younger generation takes on what we’re doing.” Show comments 1 Advertisement From Our Partners Advertisement Advertisement Express UK DWP confirms £0 BBC TV licence bill for state pensioners over 75 Express UK State pensioners over 65 handed £1,000 boost in July under Andy Burnham Mirror UK Five dead and dozens missing after horror inferno on ferry carrying 285 people The Guardian Kremlin connections: the Russia links to a £600m UK theme park Express UK Met Office names 32 areas facing heavy rain on Tuesday - full list Express UK Met Office issues ‘showers and thunderstorms' update for next week Advertisement Contact Feedback Help Cookie Policy EU Digital Services Act Terms and Privacy Policy Privacy Dashboard About Our Ads About Us Sitemap

https://www.dw.com/en/thousands-attend-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IUvT Tens of thousands of people attended Prague's Pride march Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Tens of thousands of people marched through Czech capital of Prague on Saturday as part of LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations . The festival is to last for a week. The theme of this year's event is "Times are changing." At the start of the parade, participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the Cristopher Street Day (CSD) parade in Berlin two weeks ago. The July 25 attack killed one person and injured around 31 others. Police said hundreds of officers were deployed to secure the parade route and added there were no major incidents Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK Photo/IMAGO The Saturday march in Prague was accompanied by enhanced security measures, including the deployment of hundreds of police officers and a de-escalation team. Participants were also told to carry banners by hand or to use plastic poles rather than wooden poles. "As every year, the aim of the festival is to raise awareness of LGBT+ issues, to show how this community lives in the Czech Republic and that it is still waiting for equal rights," the director of Prague Pride, Kamila Frohlichova, was cited by Germany's DPA news agency as saying. Marchers in Prague paid their respects to the victims of a car ramming in Berlin in late July Image: Michal Cizek/AFP What else do we know about the Pride march in Prague? According to police reports, there were no major incidents. A group of counter-demonstrators also gathered along part of the march's trajectory. The march began at Wenceslas Square in central Prague around noon (10:00 UTC/GMT) and arrived at Stvanice island in the Vltava River that passes through the city at around 2:30 p.m. local time, according to Czech media. A musical program was held once the march reached its terminus and the festivities continued into the night. Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Toñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire. Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas Guardians View image in fullscreen Toñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire. Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas Guardians Whales Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds Marine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered population Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.07 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spanish officials have launched an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot by a pellet gun. On Friday, Spain’s environment ministry said Toñi, the oldest living member of the pod, had been seen swimming in the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun”. Humpbacks return to Rio: the whales are back from the brink of extinction – but will tourism help or hinder? Read more A source from the ministry told El País that some of the projectiles remained lodged in her fin, posing a risk of infection. The ministry was in touch with officials in Portugal, the source added, as the markings were detected after the orcas had travelled from the waters off the Portuguese city of Faro. The orcas of the Iberian Peninsula burst into headlines in 2020 after sailors shared stories of rudders that had been rammed and boats that had been spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. Since then, a small group of orcas from the pod have been blamed for damaging scores of vessels and sinking at least four boats, leaving scientists scrambling to explain the baffling behaviour. Scientists have long pushed back against the assertion that the orcas are attacking vessels, instead suggesting that the behaviour could be a form of play or a means of practising their hunting skills. In the days since Toñi’s injuries came to light, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) association have been closely tracking the animal for any sign of weakness. “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” the IOG co-founder Janek Andre said. “Seeing Toñi, la abuela [the grandmother], like this is devastating,” he added. “If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.” Researchers have long sought to highlight the many stressors faced by this population of orcas as they navigate life in a major shipping route. Food scarcity, injuries and pollution have left the population on a knife’s edge, reduced to between 30 and 40 individuals. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion In 2023, video emerged that appeared to show people launching firecrackers into the sea as orcas rammed the rudder of their vessel, hinting that the animals were now facing another threat as sailors push back against their actions. “There has been enormous public discussion about Iberian orcas and their interactions with vessels,” said Andre. “Whatever someone’s opinion about those interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be an acceptable response. These orcas need protection, not retaliation.” Explore more on these topics Whales Spain Europe Cetaceans Marine life Wildlife news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UK waters hit with extreme heatwave as global sea temperatures reach record levels The rise of blue-space therapy: how the sea is helping people deal with trauma, anxiety and addiction Ocean surface temperatures hit a record high for June Tiny Antarctic sea creature could be key to treating melanoma, researchers say ‘Chock full of incredible animals’: marine expedition uncovers 31 new species in two weeks Magnus the wandering walrus leaves Scotland for Norway Bioluminescent algae’s blue light harnessed to make 3D-printed shapes Plan to allow fishing around Chagos Islands alarms conservationists The influencer racing to save Thailand’s most endangered sea mammal Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/kaja-kal.text: While actively running the EU’s foreign policy on the world’s most demanding issues, Kaja Kallas still finds time outside work to read about … more foreign policy. The top EU diplomat and former Estonian prime minister frequently talks about her love of reading, citing her favorite authors in speeches and meeting with them privately to discuss their work. Since taking up her most recent post in December 2024, she has read at least 52 books she has shared publicly — all of which she has posted on her Instagram — most of them related to international affairs. In total, she has shared more than 200 titles since 2017. “You know, my reading list is quite long,” said Kallas, who officially serves as the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, at a press conference in January. “By the end, when I finish this job, I will be very smart,” she joked. Advertisement The collection closely tracks the subjects Kallas is most involved with in her role, evolving alongside her professional remit: 24 books on Russia and Ukraine, nine on China, and seven on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Further-flung regions pop up only rarely, with just three books on the rest of East Asia and none on South American politics beyond Venezuela. “Reading books is a valuable advantage, especially as it is not so common nowadays,” an official from Kallas’ team told POLITICO. “The Middle East wars, Russia’s aggression and China’s growing influence are major geopolitical issues, so naturally they feature on the High Representative’s reading list.” Noting that she meets with ministers, officials, staff and experts daily and receives countless briefing papers, memos and other sources of information, “books are a nice addition on long-distance flights,” the official added. The reading lists alone have not shaped the full contours of Kallas’ foreign policy, of course. But they provide a view into which political subjects Europe’s chief diplomat is interested in learning more about and where she goes looking for answers. So, what does Kallas’ bookshelf reveal about the person shaping Europe’s diplomacy? To find out, POLITICO reviewed the 248 titles she has included on public reading lists since 2017 and spoke to 24 of the authors. Noted bookworm Kallas is not the only avid reader in Brussels, but few politicians talk about their love of literature quite as often. Since 2023, she has released reading lists twice a year on Instagram, and before that, she blogged about her latest reads monthly. “I read a lot, but you’re always influenced by the books you’ve read most recently,” Kallas told POLITICO in 2025. Political scientist Ivan Krastev, who co-authored 2019’s “The Light That Failed: A Reckoning” on why liberalism failed to spread in Eastern Europe, said Kallas had reached out to him after reading his book. She was trying to find a publisher to translate it into her native Estonian, he told POLITICO. The translation was eventually released in 2022. While Kallas was prime minister, her government had similarly pushed for the translation of political scientist Mark Leonard’s “The Age of Unpeace: How Connectivity Causes Conflict,” which she said she would “often cite.” “It’s interesting, particularly when a politician in a high position reads a book,” said Krastev. “They’re trying to make sense of their own experience” and “trying to answer some of the questions that [they] are struggling with.” Indeed, Kallas’ book choices appear to closely reflect her scheduled diplomatic trips. Visiting Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in June this year, the top diplomat had read the memoirs of Richard Holbrooke, architect of the 1995 Dayton Accords in Bosnia, and Martti Ahtisaari, the former Finnish president and mediator of the 1999 Kumanovo Agreement forcing Serbia’s withdrawal from Kosovo. A post shared by Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) “A lot to learn also today, and actually a lot of parallels,” said Kallas of Holbrooke’s book in July. Ahead of her trip to Sarajevo a month later, she then contacted former Swedish Prime Minister and High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina Carl Bildt about his 1998 book “Peace Journey: The Struggle for Peace in Bosnia,” a memoir about his work in the region. “She sent me a text and said, ‘I’m reading your book, and I like it very much.’ And I said, ‘How on earth did you get hold of that one?'” Bildt told POLITICO, joking that the book was published nearly three decades ago. “She wanted to go down into the weeds of the history … and that could be useful.” Earlier in the year, after the U.S. forcibly captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Kallas picked up two books about the South American country, too: “Comandante: Hugo Chávez’s Venezuela” and “Things Are Never So Bad That They Can’t Get Worse: Inside the Collapse of Venezuela.” “She is one of the best-read people I know,” said Marietje Schaake, a friend and former liberal MEP who served with Kallas in the European Parliament. “That depth has shaped her thinking and her career.” What’s in the library? Six of the authors who spoke to POLITICO for this article specifically cited Kallas’ hawkish stance on Moscow as echoing the messages in their books — perhaps unsurprising given Kallas warned of Russia’s threat to Europe back in 2021, during her first term as prime minister. “What is happening in Ukraine right now is what I was reading about in our own history books,” she told Vogue Greece in 2023. Sylvie Kauffmann, author of 2023’s “Blindsided” ( Les aveuglés ) — which argues that Germany and France failed to recognize the Russian threat — told POLITICO her book “confirms everything that Kallas thinks” about how others downplayed Moscow’s aggression. Speaking to POLITICO about his 2018 book “Identity,” famed political philosopher of liberal democracy Francis Fukuyama said the work contained “a kind of ideological roadmap to be able to better explain what it is that … we’re fighting for.” Noting that Ukraine’s fight against Russia was one of the reasons he wrote it, Fukuyama then praised the chief diplomat’s support for the country. Kallas has also read extensively on Israel-Palestine, a conflict on which her stance has attracted both attention and controversy in Brussels. Far more critical of Israel than her peers in the European Commission, Kallas reportedly compared the situation on the ground to South Africa under apartheid during a closed-door meeting in June, causing Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar to sever contact. Two of the authors on the subject who feature on Kallas’ reading lists told POLITICO her reported comparison mirrored the arguments made in their books, with 2024 Pulitzer Prize winner Nathan Thrall saying his “aim in writing [“A Day in the Life of Abed Salama: Anatomy of a Jerusalem Tragedy”] was to influence people like her.” “The fact that she has come to the conclusion that Israel is practicing apartheid is most welcome as far as I’m concerned,” he said. “I explain the aspects of apartheid, and I hope she’d see that her judgment is well founded,” echoed Michael Scott-Baumann, author of “Palestinians and Israelis: A Short History of Conflict.” But not every author on Kallas’ lists approves of her foreign policy decisions when it comes to their topics of specialization. Kim Ghattas, who wrote her book “Black Wave” on the Middle East, for example, said Kallas has been too passive on the Israeli-U.S. war with Iran. “That is not good policymaking. I would hope that reading books like mine can help prepare policymakers like her, specifically for moments like the one that we find ourselves in right now.” A post shared by Kaja Kallas (@kajakallas) Former U.S. National Security Adviser John Bolton, who has long advocated for regime change in Iran, said he, too, wished Kallas had become more involved — though in support of President Donald Trump’s military operation. He also noted that Kallas’ blunt style risked further alienating the U.S. from the EU, with her comments advocating for the bloc’s sovereignty “giving [Trump] the excuse to do what he probably wants to do anyway.” Criticism extended beyond the Middle East as well. Robert D. Kaplan, author of 1993’s “Balkan Ghosts” — which heavily influenced former U.S. President Bill Clinton’s initial reluctance to militarily intervene in the region, according to his biographers — told POLITICO that Kallas’ impolitic moments “may be things that she’ll come to partially regret over time.” “When you get far quick, you tend to make mistakes. Because you’re confident, you’re even arrogant,” said Kaplan. Booking ahead It’s not all about world affairs and global diplomacy, though — some of Kallas’ more recent political predicaments lie a little closer to home. Recent months have seen the top diplomat losing a turf war with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen over the bloc’s foreign policy, while her diplomatic service, the European External Action Service, has struggled to build consensus across a divided Europe. So with the rentrée almost upon us in Brussels, there may be no better time for Kallas to get through a few more books — a strategy she has turned to previously. While serving as prime minister, during a 2023 podcast, Kallas recalled how she once considered foreign policy to be her greatest political weakness — until she turned to books. “It’s not my weakness anymore because I’ve read so much about this,” she said. Perhaps this time it will be Brussels that sends her back to the stacks.

https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/in.text: Estonia Probes Russia Link in Fire at Defense Manufacturer August 19, 2026 by Ott Tammik Estonian authorities are investigating potential Russian involvement in a fire that broke out at a building used by defense company Milrem Robotics, according to Prime Minister Kristen Michal. The prosecutor’s office said on Tuesday it suspected an arson attack at the facilities of the UAE investor-backed manufacturer of autonomous combat vehicles with close ties to Ukraine. “One version being checked is that it may have been an act of sabotage and that Russia was behind the arson,” Michal said in a Facebook post. “If the purpose of this act was to intimidate Estonia, to put our people at odds with each other, or to make us stop supporting Ukraine, then it will not succeed.” Read more: Russia Is Already Waging Hybrid War in Europe, Latvia Says Authorities have identified the suspects and have requested their arrest, according to the prime minister. Nobody was injured in the fire, he said. Europe has seen an uptick in suspicious activities linked to Russia in recent years, including unauthorized drone flights, assassination attempts and incidents of sabotage. Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics said on Monday that Russia’s hybrid war on the continent has already begun. The Russian embassy in London on Monday warned that the UK would face “consequences for which it will have to answer” after reports that Kyiv used drones made by British companies to carry out strikes inside Russian territory. Milrem Robotics, majority-owned by the UAE’s EDGE Group, has supplied Ukraine with unmanned ground vehicles. In June, the company opened a production line in the Netherlands under which the Dutch government will fund 100 additional vehicles for Ukraine. “We must take into account Russia’s possible provocations and non-military threats,” Margo Palloson, Director General of the Estonian Internal Security Service, said in a statement. “Russia represents a long-term existential threat to Estonia.” Photograph: Milrem Robotics’ drone vehicles awaiting shipment at the startup’s facility in Tallinn, Estonia in 2025; photo credit: Peter Kollanyi/Bloomberg Related: War Overtakes Civil Unrest as Top Political Violence Exposure for Global Businesses Was this article valuable? https://artdaily.com/news/200745/Igor-Ho.text: Home Last Week Artists Architects Galleries Museums Photographers Photography PhotoGallery Games Subscribe Comments Search Contact Igor Hosnedl returns to London with unsettling, metaphysical works Igor Hosnedl, Untitled, 2021. Ink on paper. Framed, 54.5 x 43.5 cm. 21.46 x 17.13 in. LONDON .- PM/AM presents Exhibition 68, a solo presentation by Czech artist Igor Hosnedl (b. 1988, Uherské Hradiště; based in Berlin). The exhibition brings together a selection of works on paper made around 2021 with paintings from the same period and more recent works, offering a view across different moments of the artist’s practice. Exhibition 68 marks Hosnedl’s return to PM/AM following Exhibition 10. The drawings on view date from the same period as Rapunzel, Hosnedl’s 2021 solo exhibition at hunt kastner in Prague. Taking the Brothers Grimm tale as its starting point, the exhibition approached the story not as an illustration but as a way of exploring ambiguity that runs through the artist’s work: childlike naiveté alongside a sense of dread, stories that resist clear resolution. When critic Eva Skopalová wrote about the series, she identified the logic in ornament itself: hair, line and narrative intertwine, looping back rather than progressing in a single direction. This idea offers a useful entry point into the drawing on view: precise in touch but remains deliberately open in meaning. Each work is considered as still lifes, though not in a fixed or traditional sense. Instead, they resemble an abandoned stage, suspended between something that has just happened and something yet to come. Mechanical fragments, animal bodies, vessels, fragments of landscape and human figures gather in an ambiguous, unsettling quietness. It occupies a space that Hosnedl describes as ‘slow time’, registered in the cast shadows and empty corners of the room. A recurring curtain introduces a sense of threshold. Figures positioned as if they were uncertain guardians of what lies beyond: a landscape that has not yet taken its final form. Running through the series, there is a preoccupation about the body’s vulnerability as clothing, gestures and social roles are portrayed as forms of protection. When those elements fall away, fragility comes into view, alongside something less expected: a sense of resolve. Working at a small scale with a clear affinity for automatic drawing, Hosnedl develops these compositions through a process of reduction and stylisation. Totemic figures, objects and fragments of landscape are distilled into a precise graphic vocabulary and placed within theatrical, symbolically charged spaces. His works recall the stage-like quality of Metaphysical painting, while also drawn to a visual language shaped by graphic design and digital gaming imagery. This same linear foundation is carried into the monumental scale paintings. The hard outlines and darker tones contribute to Hosnedl’s Surrealist and Pittura Metafisica aesthetic, creating a visual language that remains open and unrestricted. Through the use of symbolic composition, the artist allows elements of the subconscious to emerge, leaving their meaning deliberately ambiguous and open to interpretation by the viewer. The paintings in the exhibition come from two distinct periods, yet a continuous thread connects them to the drawings. In Diver’s Break, the figure suspended between water and land undresses in a single, uninterrupted gesture, bringing the drawings’ preoccupation with direct exposure. In Wolf Mother, the enclosed spaces of the still lifes become fully immersive by giving the animal motif a heavier, almost archetypal presence, poised between tenderness and threat. Hosnedl has spoken of his affinity with Czech Symbolism, particularly with Jan Preisler’s Black Lake, where the landscape becomes less of a physical place than a psychological state and the human presence appears not as a master of the scene but as a temporary and vulnerable body. That sensibility between the human and its surroundings runs through the exhibition as a whole. Hosnedl’s paintings are built from handmade pigments, ground and mixed by the artist and applied with glue and damar varnish. The technique gives the surfaces a particular density and sheen, recalling the material presence of old master still lifes or icon painting rather than conventional contemporary art practice. The works on paper are executed in ink measuring 54.5 × 43.5 cm, a scale that allows the linear quality of the drawings to remain immediate, while the paintings extend into larger proportions for a more immersive space. PMAM_Exhibition 68 Igor Hosnedl Igor Hosnedl studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague (2007–2013), in the Drawing Studio of Professor Jitka Svobodová, and graduated from the studio of Vladimír Skrepl and Jiří Kovanda. He has been represented by Galerie EIGEN+ART since 2019 and by hunt kastner, Prague. In 2020, he was awarded a residency at The Fores Project, London. Recent solo exhibitions include Milky Way, Galerie EIGEN+ART, Leipzig (2026); Night Tide, Nicodim, Los Angeles (2025); DIVE, Galerie EIGEN+ART, Berlin (2024); Belladonna Harvest, Kunsthalle Bratislava (2023); Born in a Blue Body, Galerie EIGEN+ART, Leipzig (2023); and Rapunzel, hunt kastner, Prague (2021). His work was recently included in Memory of Touch at Kunsthalle Praha (2026), and has also been shown at Ribot Gallery, Milan; Downs & Ross, New York; Horizont Galéria, Budapest; FAIT Gallery, Brno; and X Museum, Beijing, among others. This is Hosnedl’s second exhibition with PM/AM, following Exhibition 10.
